questions.text: Why does the Elo system map rating differences through a logistic-like function when computing the expected score?
options: To turn rating differences into a probability between 0 and 1 that reflects win likelihood, with diminishing impact for large gaps.
To scale rating gaps so that equal differences always yield the same update magnitude regardless of outcome.
To ensure the higher-rated player always gains points no matter the match result.
To compress rating differences into a fixed bounded range while preserving their relative ordering.
questions.explanation: The function produces a win probability and saturates for large gaps, so surprise drives meaningful updates.

questions.text: What role does the K-factor play in the Elo rating update ΔR = K × (S − E)?
options: It controls how much each game outcome moves a player’s rating.
It balances ratings across different rating pools in the system.
It ensures ratings remain on an absolute fixed scale over time.
It scales the expected score E to always equal 0.5 for balanced matches.
questions.explanation: K is the sensitivity constant: larger K yields bigger rating changes per unit of surprise (S−E).

questions.text: Why is Elo considered a zero-sum rating system?
options: Because one player’s gain in rating exactly equals the other’s loss.
Because total rating points in the pool grow over time with new players.
Because both players always gain rating when they win their match.
Because draws produce no net change in any player’s rating.
questions.explanation: In head-to-head matches the sum of rating changes is zero: one wins what the other loses.

questions.text: How does the Elo formula treat a draw result in updating ratings?
options: It assigns each player S = 0.5 and updates by K × (0.5 − E).
It treats the draw as two half-wins and two half-losses simultaneously.
It ignores the game entirely and makes no rating change for either player.
It awards full points to the lower-rated player only to balance the outcome.
questions.explanation: Draws are scored as S = 0.5; rating change is K times the difference between 0.5 and expected score.

questions.text: Why does Elo avoid re-rating the entire player pool after each game?
options: Because it uses incremental updates affecting only the two participants.
Because it recalculates ratings only once per month centrally.
Because older games permanently lock in initial ratings.
Because ratings converge without any need for further adjustments.
questions.explanation: Elo updates just the two players involved, so global re-computation isn’t needed.

questions.text: What does the term (S − E) represent in the Elo update?
options: The surprise factor: how much the actual result differed from expectation.
The normalized score ratio between performance and opponent strength.
The scaled K-factor that adjusts ratings based on historic results.
The capped difference used to limit maximum rating gains per game.
questions.explanation: (S−E) measures surprise: positive if over-performing, negative if under-performing, driving the update.

questions.text: How does increasing the K-factor affect the volatility of player ratings?
options: It increases volatility by making ratings change more per game.
It decreases volatility by smoothing out rating adjustments.
It maintains the same volatility regardless of match outcomes.
It delays rating updates until a player has multiple games.
questions.explanation: A larger K makes each result swing ratings more, so volatility increases.

questions.text: Why might a tournament organizer choose a lower K for highly rated players?
options: To reduce rating swings and avoid large updates from any single match.
To accelerate rating changes so that new results matter more.
To average the ratings of all participants at the tournament end.
To penalize draws more heavily relative to decisive results.
questions.explanation: Lowering K damps single-game upsets, keeping top players’ ratings more stable.

questions.text: What assumption underlies the expected score formula E = 1 / (1 + 10^(–Δ/400))?
options: That rating differences correspond to the log-odds of winning.
That player performance follows a uniform distribution each game.
That match outcomes depend only on absolute rating magnitudes.
That ratings should change in equal increments per victory.
questions.explanation: Elo models rating gap as log-odds, so the formula is a logistic mapping to win probability.

questions.text: How could you adjust Elo for a game format with frequent draws?
options: Lower the K or modify S-scores to reflect draw frequency realistically.
Ignore draws entirely and treat them as losses for both players.
Increase base ratings uniformly to account for draw-heavy play.
Hold draws to be replayed until someone wins the match.
questions.explanation: In draw-heavy contexts you typically reduce K or tweak scoring so updates remain meaningful.

questions.text: What does a paired comparison model primarily try to estimate?
options: Each competitor’s hidden skill based on head-to-head outcomes.
The total number of wins each competitor has collected.
A fixed ranking decided before any matches are played.
The average score across team-based competitions.
questions.explanation: It infers latent skill values from pairwise match results rather than using raw win counts or preset ranks.

questions.text: Why might you see a cycle like A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A in real results?
options: Because the model enforces cycles to keep rankings dynamic.
Because match outcomes are noisy and do not always follow strict transitivity.
Because players always improve after a loss automatically.
Because previous results are discarded, causing contradictions.
questions.explanation: Real-world outcomes include randomness, so transitivity can break and cycles appear; the model reconciles them when fitting skills.

questions.text: If Alice beats Bob 8 out of 10 times, what inference does the model make?
options: Alice likely has a higher inferred skill than Bob.
Bob is assumed to be more skilled due to the remaining losses.
They are considered equally skilled because ten games are insufficient.
The system resets both players’ skills after that series.
questions.explanation: Frequent wins imply stronger evidence that Alice’s latent skill exceeds Bob’s.

questions.text: How does the model deal with all pairwise results when estimating skills?
options: It only uses the most recent result and ignores earlier ones.
It fits them simultaneously to find skill values best explaining the full set.
It averages the win rates for each pair separately without global coordination.
It randomly drops some comparisons to simplify computation.
questions.explanation: Global fitting reconciles conflicting and complementary evidence to produce consistent skill estimates.

questions.text: Why is regularization applied when few comparisons exist?
options: To keep skill estimates from becoming extreme with limited data.
To force the model to ignore all existing results.
To rank players by arbitrary fixed buckets instead of data.
To inflate the influence of early wins.
questions.explanation: Regularization tethers estimates so sparse evidence doesn’t produce overconfident or extreme skill values.

questions.text: If two players never played each other directly, how can their relative skill be inferred?
options: Transitively through common opponents' comparisons.
They are assigned the same default skill forever.
Their skills remain unknown and unused.
The model randomly chooses their relative ordering.
questions.explanation: Indirect evidence via chains of comparisons enables transitive inference of relative skill.

questions.text: Why do humans often prefer paired comparisons over absolute scoring?
options: Because absolute scores require more memory to store.
Because paired comparisons ignore any skill differences.
Because the system automatically ranks without any input.
Because it's easier to judge who is better between two than assign a number.
questions.explanation: Relative judgments reduce subjective scaling difficulty compared to assigning absolute values.

questions.text: What effect does increasing the number of comparisons between the same pair have?
options: It forces their skills to converge to the same value.
It increases the likelihood of discarding earlier data.
It reduces uncertainty in their relative skill estimate.
It makes the model ignore that pair in future updates.
questions.explanation: More data tightens the estimate, decreasing variance around their inferred skill difference.

questions.text: How can ties be represented in a paired comparison model?
options: They are treated as wins for both players.
As a partial outcome (e.g., half-win) or with a tie probability.
They are deleted from the history automatically.
They are converted into a random winner to simplify modeling.
questions.explanation: Explicitly modeling ties preserves that information without forcing a decisive result.

questions.text: Why might recent match outcomes be weighted more heavily?
options: To reflect changes in player ability over time.
To discard older evidence entirely as irrelevant.
To keep early matches dominant in all future estimates.
To prevent any updates to the skill values.
questions.explanation: Weighting recent results more allows the model to adapt if skills shift over time.

2.description:
Measures how spread out values are around the mean. Calculated as:

σ = √( (1/N) Σᵢ (xᵢ – μ)² )

In a Gaussian (normal) distribution, σ sets the scale: about 68% of values lie within ±1σ, 95% within ±2σ, and 99.7% within ±3σ. Saying “1 standard deviation away” means one σ unit from the mean—it scales with the dataset. In rating systems, this concept becomes “rating deviation” (RD): both are σ-style uncertainty measures, but standard deviation describes the spread of a dataset, while RD quantifies uncertainty in an individual player’s rating. RD decreases with more game results (more confidence) and increases during inactivity (less recent information). Example: if ratings follow a normal curve centered at 1500 with σ=100, ~68% of players score between 1400 and 1600.

questions.text: What does standard deviation tell you about a dataset?
options: The average value of the dataset.
The proportion of values above the mean.
How far typical values are from the mean, i.e., the dataset's spread.
The difference between the highest and lowest values.
questions.explanation: Standard deviation quantifies dispersion: how much values typically deviate from the mean.

questions.text: If every value in a dataset is identical, what is the standard deviation?
options: The average value of the dataset.
Undefined, since variance cannot be computed.
Zero, because there is no variation.
Very large, because uniformity hides spread.
questions.explanation: With no difference from the mean, all deviations are zero, so σ is zero.

questions.text: Why are differences squared when computing variance (the step before taking the square root)?
options: To make the number smaller only for display purposes.
To convert the values into probabilities.
To prevent positive and negative deviations from canceling and to emphasize larger gaps.
To simplify the arithmetic by removing decimals.
questions.explanation: Squaring avoids cancellation of signs and gives greater weight to larger deviations.

questions.text: Why do we take the square root after averaging squared deviations?
options: Because without it the variance would be negative.
To return to the original units so spread is interpretable.
To make the result always less than one.
To reduce the influence of large deviations arbitrarily.
questions.explanation: The square root brings the measure back to the same units as the data, making interpretation easier.

questions.text: In a normal distribution, roughly what proportion lies within one standard deviation of the mean?
options: About 95%, since most data points cluster tightly.
About 50%, the median spread.
About 68%, reflecting moderate deviations being common.
Nearly 100%, because σ covers almost all values.
questions.explanation: For a Gaussian, ~68% of values fall within ±1σ of the mean.

questions.text: What impact does an outlier have on standard deviation?
options: It makes σ negative due to skew.
It has no effect if the dataset has many points.
It increases σ because its large squared deviation adds heavily.
It decreases σ by pulling the mean toward itself.
questions.explanation: Outliers produce large deviations that, when squared, inflate the overall spread.

questions.text: If you add the same constant to every data point, how does standard deviation change?
options: It stays the same, since relative differences are unchanged.
It halves because the mean shifts.
It becomes zero, as values become more uniform.
It increases by that constant amount.
questions.explanation: Adding a constant shifts all points equally; dispersion about the mean remains identical.

questions.text: If you multiply every value in the dataset by a positive constant c, what happens to σ?
options: It remains unchanged regardless of scaling.
It is divided by c, compressing the spread.
It is multiplied by c, scaling the spread accordingly.
It becomes squared like the variance.
questions.explanation: Scaling data by c scales standard deviation by the same factor, preserving relative structure.

questions.text: How is standard deviation different from rating deviation (RD) in a rating system?
options: They are exactly the same; the terms are interchangeable.
RD is always smaller because it tracks individual players.
Standard deviation only applies to ratings, while RD is for general statistics.
Standard deviation describes dataset spread; RD is uncertainty of a single player’s rating that evolves with activity.
questions.explanation: RD reflects confidence in one rating over time, whereas σ is a static measure of overall data spread.

questions.text: Why does rating deviation increase when a player is inactive?
options: Because the player’s rating is reset to the mean automatically.
Because lack of recent results raises uncertainty, so RD grows to reflect less confidence.
Because old games are removed, reducing evidence.
Because the system locks the rating, preventing any change.
questions.explanation: Inactivity means no new information; uncertainty about true skill increases, raising RD.

questions.text: Why prefer the logistic-style mapping over a simple linear rescaling when turning score differences into probabilities?
options: Because it ensures that outputs stay bounded within the [0,1] range.
Because linear scaling requires more arithmetic operations and is slower.
Because only logistic produces exact 0 or 1 values for extreme inputs.
Because it always gives equal weight to all differences regardless of magnitude.
questions.explanation: Logistic keeps outputs bounded and reduces sensitivity for extreme gaps, which models uncertainty and surprise appropriately.

questions.text: What does the midpoint (x = 0) of the logistic function represent in probability terms?
options: A guaranteed win for the higher input.
An ignored input because it's neutral.
Equal odds: probability 0.5 (maximum uncertainty).
Certainty in outcome because the curve flattens.
questions.explanation: At x=0 the logistic output is 0.5, meaning both sides are equally likely; it's the most uncertain point.

questions.text: Why is it useful that the logistic function saturates (flattens) for very large positive or negative inputs?
options: Because it reduces the impact of already-certain outcomes and avoids overreacting.
Because it makes the function more linear in the tails.
Because saturation introduces randomness in predictions.
Because it forces all inputs to map to exactly 0 or 1 beyond a threshold.
questions.explanation: Saturation means extreme differences produce probabilities near certainty but don’t overshoot, so updates shrink when outcome is unsurprising.

questions.text: What does the derivative of the logistic function tell you about its behavior?
options: The cumulative probability up to a given input.
How far the output is from 1 in absolute terms.
The point where the curve crosses the x-axis.
How sensitive the output probability is to small changes in input, largest near the midpoint.
questions.explanation: The derivative measures sensitivity; logistic is most responsive around x=0 and flattens in the tails.

questions.text: Why would you apply a logistic transformation when combining model features to produce a probability?
options: To create a hard cutoff so outputs are strictly 0 or 1.
To smoothly compress arbitrary outputs into [0,1].
To avoid having to normalize the data beforehand.
To amplify extreme feature values disproportionately.
questions.explanation: Logistic makes arbitrary scores interpretable as probabilities while remaining differentiable for optimization.

questions.text: Why does the Elo expected score formula divide the rating difference Δ by 400 before applying 10 to that power?
options: To calibrate the scale so a 400-point gap corresponds to about a 10:1 win odds, yielding sensible probabilities.
To compress all rating differences into the [0,1] range before the logistic step.
To guarantee the expected score is exactly 0.5 when ratings are equal.
To make rating differences additive in probability space without further transformation.
questions.explanation: Dividing by 400 sets the sensitivity: a 400-point difference gives 10^(1)=10 odds ratio, mapping to ≈0.91 win probability, which is a chosen calibration of skill gaps.

questions.text: What happens if you decrease the denominator in the exponent (e.g., use 200 instead of 400) in the Elo-style logistic?
options: The curve steepens, smaller rating gaps push probabilities closer to 0 or 1.
The curve flattens, making it less responsive to differences.
Output probabilities are no longer bounded between 0 and 1.
It inverts the meaning of strong and weak players.
questions.explanation: Reducing the scale makes the logistic transition sharper, increasing sensitivity to rating differences.

questions.text: When might the logistic function be a poor model for converting a score to a probability?
options: When you need a smooth transition without any saturation.
When outcomes are completely deterministic and require no uncertainty modeling.
When you want to allow probabilities outside [0,1] for flexibility.
When the relationship is asymmetric or violates constant odds-ratio assumptions, so its symmetric S-shape misfits the data.
questions.explanation: Logistic assumes symmetry in log-odds; if real behavior has asymmetrical tail behavior or changing odds ratios, it can misrepresent probabilities.

questions.text: Why is logistic preferable to a step function for mapping a continuous score to a probability in a learning context?
options: Because it provides a graded, smooth output that reflects uncertainty instead of an abrupt yes/no.
Because step functions are differentiable and easier to tune.
Because logistic always outputs integers.
Because subtle changes in input have no effect on the output.
questions.explanation: Logistic gives gradual shifts in belief, which is useful for incremental learning and avoids brittle decisions.

questions.text: If you have independent pieces of evidence in log-odds form, why add them before applying logistic instead of averaging their probabilities?
options: Averaging probabilities always biases toward 0.5, whereas adding log-odds loses information.
Because probabilities cannot be combined at all without logistic.
Because adding log-odds multiplies the underlying odds, and logistic of the sum yields the correct combined probability.
Because logistic requires inputs to be equal before combining.
questions.explanation: Log-odds combine additively for independent evidence; applying logistic after summing gives the updated probability consistently.

questions.text: What is the primary innovation of Glicko compared to basic Elo?
options: It periodically recalculates all player ratings in batch to keep the system consistent.
It tracks uncertainty (RD) alongside the rating, making confidence explicit.
It removes the need for expected scores by using fixed updates.
It only updates ratings after a fixed number of games to reduce noise.
questions.explanation: Glicko augments a player’s rating with a rating deviation (RD) that quantifies uncertainty, enabling more informed updates and interpretations.

questions.text: Why does a player’s RD grow during periods of inactivity?
options: Because the system resets RD to maximum after inactivity to avoid outdated confidence.
Because uncertainty increases assuming the player's rating is now unreliable.
Because the player's rating is reduced linearly over time to reflect decay.
Because past game results are discarded and averaged again.
questions.explanation: Without recent games, the system becomes less certain about true skill; RD grows by adding variance to reflect that increased uncertainty.

questions.text: How does Glicko combine prior uncertainty and new game data when updating RD after a match?
options: By taking the larger of the prior and new deviation to stay conservative.
By replacing the old RD entirely if the new data is more recent.
By summing precisions (inverse variances) and inverting: RD_new = √(1 / (1/RD² + 1/d²)).
By averaging old and new deviations equally.
questions.explanation: Independent sources combine by adding precision; the harmonic-like formula yields a reduced RD reflecting increased certainty from both prior and new data.

questions.text: What does a large rating deviation (RD) imply about a player?
options: The player has a very stable rating with minimal expected change.
The player consistently defeats higher-rated opponents.
The player has a high recent win rate regardless of opponents.
The system is uncertain about the player's true skill.
questions.explanation: Large RD means less information has been gathered or outdated activity, so the rating is uncertain and the corresponding confidence interval is broader.

questions.text: If a player has a small RD, how does that affect their rating update after a game?
options: Updates become larger because the system trusts the rating more.
Updates become smaller because the existing rating is reliable.
The opponent’s rating increases by more due to high reliability.
The game outcome is ignored for the opponent because of uncertainty.
questions.explanation: Small RD indicates high confidence in the current rating, so new results produce smaller adjustments.

questions.text: Why does Glicko adjust the expected score computation using RD (e.g., via a weighting function like g(RD))?
options: To make expected scores always default to 0.5 when uncertainty is high.
To convert the logistic curve into a linear probability for easier mixing.
To downweight extreme rating differences when one or both players are uncertain, making predictions less overconfident.
To ensure the higher-rated player always has overwhelming predicted advantage regardless of uncertainty.
questions.explanation: The weighting softens the impact of rating differences when uncertainty is large, preventing overconfident predictions from unreliable estimates.

questions.text: What does the confidence interval r ± 1.96·RD represent in Glicko?
options: How much the player's rating will change on their next win.
The range in which the player's true skill rating lies with roughly 95% confidence.
The typical ratings of players they are expected to beat.
How many games the player can go without playing before RD doubles.
questions.explanation: Assuming normality, r ± 1.96·RD gives the interval where the true rating lies with about 95% probability, making uncertainty explicit.

questions.text: If a player with high RD beats a low-RD opponent, what is the expected effect on their rating and RD?
options: Their rating barely changes due to high uncertainty, and RD stays large.
Both players' RD increase because the result was unexpected.
Their rating moves significantly and their RD shrinks, since the result provides strong information.
The opponent loses RD while the winner’s RD remains unchanged.
questions.explanation: A win by an uncertain (high-RD) player against a confident opponent is informative: the rating adjusts noticeably and RD reduces, reflecting increased certainty.

questions.text: Why does Glicko combine variances using inverse sums (i.e., combining precision) instead of a simple average when updating uncertainty?
options: Averaging would give too much weight to old data and ignore new information.
Independent pieces of evidence combine by summing precision, yielding a tighter updated estimate.
Taking the maximum variance is safer for uncertain systems.
It makes the math simpler by treating all uncertainties linearly.
questions.explanation: Combining precision (inverse variance) is the correct method for fusing independent estimates, producing a lower overall uncertainty than naive averaging.

questions.text: In what scenario does Glicko behave similarly to Elo?
options: When no games have been played and everyone starts with equal ratings.
When large RD values make all match outcomes unpredictable.
When both players have very small RD, so uncertainty adjustments become negligible.
When the system uses a fixed update size regardless of outcome.
questions.explanation: With tiny RD (high certainty), the uncertainty-aware modifications fade and Glicko’s updates resemble Elo’s because confidence adjustments are minimal.

questions.text: What does the arithmetic mean represent in a dataset?
options: The most common value among the entries.
The sum of deviations from here is zero.
The middle value when all numbers are sorted.
The largest value in the set.
questions.explanation: The mean is defined so that positive and negative deviations cancel; it's the balancing point of the data.

questions.text: How does the arithmetic mean relate to standard deviation?
options: It normalizes standard deviation to be between 0 and 1.
It averages the variances to get the deviation.
It is the fixed reference from which squared deviations are computed for spread.
It explains why distributions are always symmetric.
questions.explanation: Standard deviation measures the average squared distance of values from the mean, so the mean is the central reference.

questions.text: If you add 5 to every number in a dataset, how does the mean change?
options: It stays the same.
It doubles.
It increases by 5.
It becomes the median.
questions.explanation: Adding a constant shifts all values equally, so the mean increases by that constant.

questions.text: If you multiply every value in a dataset by 3, how does the mean change?
options: It increases by 3.
It remains unchanged.
It increases by 3/(# of values).
It triples.
questions.explanation: Scaling all values by a factor scales the mean by the same factor.

questions.text: Why can the arithmetic mean be misleading in some datasets?
options: Because it always underestimates the central tendency.
Because outliers can skew it away from most values.
Because it only works on integer values.
Because it ignores the size of the dataset.
questions.explanation: Extreme values (outliers) can pull the mean away from where the bulk of data lies, misrepresenting a 'typical' value.

questions.text: Given chess player ratings [1400, 1500, 1600, 1700, 1800], what is their mean and what does it reflect?
options: 1500, reflecting the median better than average.
1700, showing the highest tier among them.
1600, reflecting the average skill level.
1550, because extreme values are discarded in mean.
questions.explanation: The average of those ratings is 1600; it represents the central/typical skill level of the group.

questions.text: If group A has mean 100 with 3 members and group B has mean 200 with 1 member, what's the combined mean?
options: 150, average of the two means.
125, because total sum is (300 + 200) / 4.
100, since group A dominates.
200, because group B has the highest mean.
questions.explanation: Weighted average: (3*100 + 1*200)/4 = 125; group sizes influence the combined mean.

questions.text: Why is the sum of deviations from the mean always zero?
options: Because all data points are equidistant from the mean.
Because the mean is always zero in normalized datasets.
Because the mean is the value that makes positive and negative deviations cancel out.
Because deviations are squared before summing.
questions.explanation: By definition, the mean balances the data: deviations above and below sum to zero.

questions.text: When will the arithmetic mean equal the median?
options: When there are extreme outliers.
When the distribution is symmetric.
Only when the dataset has an even number of items.
When all values are different.
questions.explanation: In symmetric distributions, the center is the same whether measured by mean or median.

questions.text: What happens to the mean if you add a new value equal to the current mean?
options: The mean increases slightly.
The mean decreases slightly.
The mean becomes that new value only.
The mean stays the same.
questions.explanation: Adding another instance of the current mean doesn't change the average.

questions.text: What property of exponential functions makes them ideal for modeling continuous growth like compound interest?
options: Their rate of change is proportional to their current value.
They add a fixed amount each interval, matching constant increases.
They stay bounded to prevent runaway growth.
They reverse direction when inputs become negative.
questions.explanation: Because the derivative is proportional to the value itself, growth accelerates and compounds continuously.

questions.text: Why does using base e simplify differentiation of exponential growth?
options: It eliminates the need to consider limits in calculus.
Powers of e approximate all polynomials without error.
Because e^x equals its own derivative.
Because e is less than 1, making expressions shrink naturally.
questions.explanation: The derivative of e^x is e^x, so no additional constants appear, simplifying analysis.

questions.text: In the logistic function L(x)=1/(1+e^{-x}), what role does the term e^{-x} play?
options: It forces the output to always stay positive by adding a constant offset.
It shrinks the denominator for large positive x and enlarges it for large negative x.
It scales x linearly so the curve passes through (0,0.5).
It makes the function oscillate around 0.5 for moderate inputs.
questions.explanation: e^{-x} modulates the denominator so the output transitions smoothly between 0 and 1 in the classic S shape.

questions.text: Why does e^{-x} decay as x increases?
options: Because e^{-x} equals 1 divided by e^{x}, so larger x makes the denominator grow and the value shrink.
Because negative exponents cause oscillations that average downward.
Because the logistic definition manually caps it to decay.
Because the base becomes less than one when the exponent is negative.
questions.explanation: e^{-x} = 1/e^{x}; as x grows, e^{x} grows, so its reciprocal decreases.

questions.text: In an exponential decay model y = y₀ * e^{-t/τ}, what does τ represent?
options: The time it takes for the quantity to halve.
The rate at which the initial amount is added over time.
The time over which the quantity falls to about 37% of its starting value.
The fixed amount subtracted each step in the decay.
questions.explanation: τ is the time constant: after τ, the value is roughly y₀/e (~37%).

questions.text: Why is taking the natural logarithm helpful when solving for time in A = A₀ e^{kt}?
options: Because ln turns the exponential into a polynomial of fixed degree.
Because ln ignores the initial amount A₀.
Because ln bounds the result between 0 and 1.
Because ln isolates the exponent, converting multiplicative growth into a linear expression.
questions.explanation: Taking ln lets you solve for t by bringing the exponent down: ln(A/A₀)=kt.

questions.text: Which explanation best captures why exponential growth eventually outpaces any fixed-degree polynomial?
options: Polynomials have a maximum beyond which they stop growing.
Exponential’s rate increases with its current value, causing accelerating growth that surpasses fixed power increases.
Polynomial degrees decrease over time while exponentials remain constant.
Exponential functions are finite sums, while polynomials are infinite.
questions.explanation: Exponential growth compounds on itself, so its speed accelerates and dominates polynomial growth.

questions.text: You observe a quantity doubling every 5 time units. Which continuous exponential expression models that?
options: y = y₀ * e^{(ln 2 / 5) t}
y = y₀ * e^{(5 ln 2) t}
y = y₀ * e^{(ln 2) / t}
questions.explanation: Doubling every 5 units means growth rate is ln(2)/5 in the continuous form.

questions.text: In the formula for continuous compounding A = P e^{rt}, what does r represent?
options: The total accumulated interest over the period.
The principal scaled per time unit.
The continuous interest rate per time unit.
The number of discrete compounding intervals.
questions.explanation: r is the instantaneous rate; compounding continuously uses e^{rt} to accumulate interest.

questions.text: Why is expressing e^x as its Taylor series around zero useful for approximations?
options: Because the series terminates for large x making it exact.
Because it turns e^x into a product of simpler functions.
Because the infinite sum converges for all x, so truncating gives good approximations with known error.
Because it restricts e^x values to a bounded interval.
questions.explanation: The series converges everywhere, letting you approximate e^x by summing a few terms.

questions.text: What is the main goal of a statistical model?
options: To describe data visually using graphs and charts.
To explain how data are generated and make predictions using parameterized assumptions.
To store datasets for long-term archival.
To apply deterministic rules for computing fixed outcomes.

questions.text: How does a statistical model treat the concept of uncertainty?
options: It ignores uncertainty and assumes all parameters are known.
It uses fixed equations to eliminate randomness in observed data.
It incorporates uncertainty through probability distributions over parameters or outcomes.
It adds noise manually to simulate real-world variation.

questions.text: In a paired comparison model like Glicko, what are the parameters being estimated?
options: The number of games each player has played.
The skill levels of players, often treated as latent variables.
The frequency of wins and losses in the data.
The identities of opponents in each match.

questions.text: Why do statistical models often assume a distribution like the Gaussian?
options: Because it makes the math more complicated and realistic.
Because it's the only distribution that works with real data.
Because many natural processes cluster around a mean with symmetric variation, making Gaussian a useful default.
Because computers are optimized to simulate Gaussian noise.

questions.text: What does 'fitting a statistical model to data' mean?
options: Manually adjusting values to match a plot.
Picking a random function and applying it to the dataset.
Choosing parameters that best explain observed data under the model’s assumptions.
Using brute force to memorize all outcomes.

questions.text: Why are statistical models useful in rating systems?
options: They let us encode animations for performance visualizations.
They help determine exact win conditions for players.
They allow structured updates to skill estimates based on observed results.
They remove the need for any randomness in player outcomes.

questions.text: What is a key difference between a deterministic model and a statistical model?
options: Deterministic models require less code to implement.
Statistical models account for uncertainty and randomness in data.
Deterministic models are better for real-time applications.
Statistical models never change once defined.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the role of data in a statistical model?
options: Data are used to validate if the model's outputs are intuitive.
Data are ignored after the model structure is defined.
Data guide the estimation of the model's unknown parameters.
Data are only useful if the sample size is infinite.

questions.text: What makes a statistical model 'probabilistic'?
options: It uses randomness to ensure unpredictable results.
It outputs probabilities or uses probability distributions to describe possible outcomes.
It requires only complete datasets to function.
It computes results by flipping a coin at each step.

questions.text: Why are parameters in statistical models often considered 'latent'?
options: Because they are selected randomly and not observed.
Because they are fixed values defined in advance.
Because they are unobserved and must be inferred from the data.
Because they represent background music in a simulation.

questions.text: What does a 95% confidence interval mean in practice?
options: There is a 95% chance the observed data fall within this range.
95% of the time, the estimated value is exactly the midpoint of the interval.
If the same experiment were repeated many times, 95% of the computed intervals would contain the true value.
The interval will always contain the true value if calculated correctly.

questions.text: Why is 1.96 commonly used when calculating a 95% confidence interval?
options: Because it corresponds to two standard deviations under the Gaussian distribution.
Because 1.96 is the value where the logistic function reaches 95%.
Because it’s the z-score capturing 95% of probability mass under the standard normal curve.
Because it is easier to calculate than 2.00 and offers greater accuracy.

questions.text: In the Glicko system, how is a confidence interval constructed for a player’s rating?
options: By multiplying their rating by 1.96.
By subtracting and adding 1.96 times their RD to/from their rating.
By finding the rating of the last 10 opponents and computing the average.
By simulating thousands of future matches and calculating the rating range.

questions.text: Why does the width of a confidence interval increase as RD increases?
options: Because larger RD means greater certainty about the estimate.
Because higher RD reflects more confidence in past results.
Because RD represents uncertainty, and wider intervals reflect less precise estimates.
Because RD accounts for rating inflation over time.

questions.text: If two players have overlapping 95% confidence intervals, what can we conclude?
options: That their exact ratings are the same.
That one player is guaranteed to be stronger than the other.
That their true skill levels may not be statistically distinguishable.
That both players will draw most matches.

questions.text: What happens to a player’s confidence interval if they stay inactive for a long time?
options: It narrows due to rating stability.
It becomes centered at zero.
It widens because RD increases with inactivity, adding uncertainty.
It disappears since there is no new data to analyze.

questions.text: Why is it more informative to report a confidence interval than just a point estimate?
options: Because it shows how random the results are.
Because it guarantees correctness of predictions.
Because it communicates both the estimate and the uncertainty around it.
Because it avoids showing sensitive numerical results.

questions.text: Which of the following would reduce the width of a player’s confidence interval over time?
options: Playing more games, reducing RD due to increased evidence.
Increasing the K-factor in their rating updates.
Resetting their rating to the population mean.
Switching to a deterministic model without randomness.

questions.text: Why is the Gaussian distribution used when constructing confidence intervals in systems like Glicko?
options: Because it matches the uniform distribution of skill across all players.
Because many real-world skill estimations are modeled with symmetric, bell-shaped uncertainty.
Because it prevents players from having negative ratings.
Because Gaussian distributions are required by Elo’s original design.

questions.text: How would you interpret a confidence interval of (1750, 1950) for a player’s rating?
options: The player’s exact rating is 1850.
Their rating is guaranteed to fall between those bounds.
We’re 95% confident their true skill lies between 1750 and 1950.
The interval predicts all future match results against other players.

questions.text: What key advantage does the streaming memory module offer SAM 2 in video segmentation?
options: It enables dynamic resizing of input frames for consistent output.
It allows cross-frame fusion of features without retraining per video.
It increases frame rate by skipping redundant pixels.
It compresses segmentation masks into lower-dimensional vectors.

questions.text: What is a 'masklet' in the context of SAM 2?
options: A short video clip pre-segmented by the model.
An interactive segmentation output for a video prompt.
A data format used to compress multiple masks.
A segmentation refinement tool integrated in the training loop.

questions.text: How does SAM 2 unify image and video segmentation?
options: By converting all videos into tiled image sequences for inference.
By using a single encoder-decoder model for both tasks.
By defining a Promptable Visual Segmentation (PVS) task that applies to both domains.
By merging all image datasets into a synthetic video corpus.

questions.text: Which architectural upgrade allows SAM 2 to handle temporal context effectively?
options: Replacing the decoder with a CNN-RNN hybrid module.
Introducing memory-attention blocks with cross-frame access.
Using only keyframes to approximate video context.
Adding dropout layers trained on motion masks.

questions.text: What does SAM 2 achieve compared to prior systems like XMem++ and Cutie?
options: Better zero-shot classification accuracy across 100+ classes.
Stronger performance in interactive segmentation with fewer user prompts.
More efficient object detection in satellite imagery.
Improved automatic captioning of segmented regions.

questions.text: What role does the Hiera encoder play in SAM 2’s architecture?
options: It converts low-resolution outputs into masklets.
It replaces all vision encoders in the model with diffusion modules.
It provides hierarchical visual features to support segmentation at multiple scales.
It transforms RGB input into one-hot semantic labels.

questions.text: What design feature enables SAM 2 to work on arbitrarily long videos?
options: A static memory of prior semantic labels.
A recursive token-generation mechanism across frames.
A streaming FIFO memory of embeddings and mask pointers.
A cache of precomputed decoder activations.

questions.text: Why is the SA-V dataset important for SAM 2?
options: It provides language prompts to train the mask decoder.
It introduces novel object categories for few-shot learning.
It enables scaling by supplying massive interactive mask data with minimal constraints.
It supports benchmarking under varying lighting and occlusion.

questions.text: How does SAM 2 maintain high performance while achieving 43.8 FPS on an A100 GPU?
options: By using low-resolution inputs and a smaller decoder.
By processing video frames in parallel GPU batches.
By combining real-time memory attention with an efficient transformer design.
By offloading most computations to a pretrained language model.

questions.text: What does it mean that SAM 2 exceeds SAM on 37 zero-shot image benchmarks?
options: SAM 2 was retrained on each dataset for fine-tuned results.
It performs better than SAM even without task-specific fine-tuning.
It uses extra annotations that SAM lacked.
Its speed compensates for any drop in accuracy.

questions.text: What does it mean that SAM is a 'promptable' segmentation model?
options: It automatically generates captions before segmenting an image.
It learns segmentation purely from user interactions.
It accepts diverse prompts like points, boxes, masks, or text to guide segmentation.
It segments predefined objects stored in a lookup table.

questions.text: What is the role of the prompt encoder in SAM’s architecture?
options: To compress the final masks into binary representations.
To embed user-provided cues like clicks or text into the segmentation pipeline.
To label masks with semantic class names after generation.
To fine-tune the model during inference based on feedback.

questions.text: What makes the SA-1B dataset released with SAM significant?
options: It was the first dataset to include semantic labels with every mask.
It introduced video-based segmentation masks.
It provided over 1.1 billion high-quality masks on 11 million privacy-safe images.
It contained 3D reconstructions from multi-view images.

questions.text: How does SAM achieve real-time segmentation performance?
options: By using only low-resolution inputs to minimize compute.
By executing all segmentation offline before user prompts.
Through an efficient combination of a ViT image encoder and a fast mask decoder.
By relying on GPU-specific hardware acceleration via CUDA kernels.

questions.text: What type of performance does SAM demonstrate on segmentation benchmarks?
options: Inferior performance due to lack of domain-specific fine-tuning.
Competitive zero-shot results across 23 tasks including edge and instance segmentation.
High accuracy only on datasets with pre-labeled bounding boxes.
State-of-the-art performance on text classification benchmarks.

questions.text: What is the primary benefit of using a fixed-size FIFO buffer in streaming memory?
options: It eliminates the need for positional embeddings in transformers.
It ensures the model has access to the entire video history.
It keeps compute and memory usage constant regardless of video length.
It preloads future frames to speed up inference.

questions.text: How does streaming memory help reduce flicker or jitter in video segmentation?
options: By downsampling mask resolution to blur rapid transitions.
By fusing recent frame features to smooth temporal inconsistencies.
By caching object labels for each segment.
By switching to static masks after detecting rapid motion.

questions.text: What happens when a new frame is added to the streaming memory buffer?
options: It replaces the frame with the highest prediction loss.
It clears the entire memory to avoid temporal bias.
It appends the new features and evicts the oldest ones.
It merges with all previous frames to form a global context.

questions.text: How does SAM 2 use streaming memory to enable prompt propagation over time?
options: It replicates prompt encodings across every frame in parallel.
It converts prompts into object tracks using k-means clustering.
It writes updated mask tokens into memory, allowing later frames to refine masks without new prompts.
It fine-tunes the model between each frame using the last prompt.

questions.text: Why doesn’t streaming memory need to store the entire video history?
options: Because earlier frames lose relevance for real-time segmentation.
Because mask quality decreases if too much context is used.
Because user prompts are only valid for the first few frames.
Because video frames are compressed and cannot be retrieved later.

questions.text: What core mechanism enables Transformers to model long-range dependencies efficiently?
options: Convolutional filters applied recursively across tokens.
Multi-head self-attention over all token pairs.
Sequential RNN gating with residual memory.
Hierarchical token pooling in a tree structure.

questions.text: Why are positional encodings necessary in a Transformer architecture?
options: To reduce overfitting in feed-forward layers.
To assign class labels to each token after decoding.
To inject order or spatial information into attention, which is permutation-invariant.
To control the dropout rate across transformer heads.

questions.text: How does multi-head attention improve a Transformer’s representational power?
options: By stacking outputs from multiple CNN backbones.
By summing the results of separate recurrent layers.
By computing different attention patterns in parallel for richer context understanding.
By applying separate positional encodings per token dimension.

questions.text: Why are Transformers a good fit for SAM 2’s segmentation tasks?
options: Because they use hand-tuned filters for edge detection.
Because their recurrent structure naturally handles video sequences.
Because they enable global attention over high-resolution inputs and flexible integration of prompts and memory.
Because they can precompute masks without image inputs.

questions.text: What is the function of the position-wise feed-forward network in a Transformer?
options: It reduces token dimensionality for faster attention.
It mixes features independently at each token to enhance local transformations.
It computes pairwise distances between all token embeddings.
It generates positional encodings dynamically during inference.

questions.text: What distinguishes deep learning from traditional machine learning methods?
options: It uses manually engineered features instead of learning them.
It relies solely on decision trees for pattern recognition.
It learns hierarchical feature representations directly from raw data through stacked layers.
It requires fewer training examples to generalize well.

questions.text: How does backpropagation enable learning in deep neural networks?
options: By converting nonlinear activations into binary decisions.
By computing gradients of the loss with respect to weights and updating them via gradient descent.
By randomly resetting weights to find better solutions.
By pruning neurons that do not activate during training.

questions.text: What role do early layers typically play in a deep neural network?
options: They encode class-specific outputs for final prediction.
They remove noise by compressing all information.
They learn low-level patterns like edges and textures.
They generate reinforcement signals for the loss function.

questions.text: Why is end-to-end differentiability important in systems like SAM 2?
options: It ensures the model uses only linear activations.
It enables all components—from input prompt to output mask—to be trained together for optimal performance.
It eliminates the need for any labeled data.
It makes the model interpretable and explainable by default.

questions.text: How does deep learning benefit SAM 2 specifically?
options: It allows SAM 2 to run without GPUs or accelerators.
It enables the model to hand-code rules for each object class.
It powers scalable feature extraction and flexible architectures.
It largely increases accuracy on zero-shot tasks compared to one-shot and few-shot.

questions.text: What is the main purpose of an image encoder?
options: To classify images into predefined categories.
To convert raw pixel data into compact feature vectors.
To convert image content to semantic descriptions.
To reconstruct high-resolution versions of compressed images.

questions.text: Why do downstream tasks like segmentation and detection rely on image encoders?
options: Because they require images to be converted to labeled data to function.
Because raw images contain too many redundant pixel values and are more efficiently stored as vectors.
Because these tasks operate more effectively on structured visual embeddings than on raw pixel values.
Because image encoders compress images to save storage space.

questions.text: What kind of information do image encoders typically capture in their outputs?
options: Only object class labels for each pixel.
Sequences of image captions and text descriptions.
Edges, textures, shapes, and contextual features.
Timestamps and camera metadata.

questions.text: How does pretraining help image encoders?
options: It teaches them to generate longer feature vectors for each image.
It enables them to memorize all possible images.
It provides a general foundation for visual understanding before fine-tuning on specific tasks.
It eliminates the need for backpropagation in training.

questions.text: What tradeoff does a good image encoder try to balance?
options: Storage cost vs. pixel fidelity.
Model size vs. latency.
Local visual detail vs. global context.
Color accuracy vs. image resolution.
